passage: The Solapur bus stopped for twenty minutes at Mohol, and Hemant jumped down, starving. Two eateries faced the stand. One was packed, benches full, people standing with plates. The other was half empty, a man frying vadas in a clean kadhai. "That one," Hemant said, pointing at the crowd. "So many people can't be wrong." Omkar raised an eyebrow. "You didn't even look at the menu." "Don't need to." They squeezed in, waited twelve minutes, and got lukewarm poha. Hemant ate fast, watching the clock. Omkar glanced out. "That crowd is all from our bus. They just followed the first ones who got down." Across the road, the vada man was finally getting customers from another bus, and the vadas looked hot.

qa.q: What did Hemant and Omkar get after waiting?
qa.a: Lukewarm poha.

qa.q: What was Hemant thinking when pointing at the crowded eatery?
qa.a: Hemant assumed a packed place must be good, treating the number of people as proof of quality.

qa.q: What quick check could Hemant have made before choosing, with only twenty minutes to spare?
qa.a: Hemant could have glanced at both kitchens and menus, like the clean kadhai and fresh vadas, instead of trusting the crowd.

qa.q: How might the vada man across the road see busy stands like the other one?
qa.a: The vada man may know that travellers follow the first few people off a bus, so a clean, good stall can sit empty just because nobody went first.

grounding: A young adult picks the crowded eatery at a bus stop without checking, taking the crowd as proof of quality.

passage: Tomas had one evening to pick a summer course before the student discount ran out. He opened the course site, sorted by rating, and there it was: Data Analysis Essentials, 4.9 stars, twelve thousand reviews. He paid without opening the syllabus. "Twelve thousand people," he told Mateo across the tiny kitchen of their flat in Valencia. "It has to be good." Mateo, stirring rice, asked, "Good for who?" Tomas waved him off. Two weeks later he was watching a video on how to open a spreadsheet. The next module explained what a column was. Tomas had used spreadsheets at his part-time job for two years. He scrolled down to the reviews and read one properly for the first time: "Perfect for total beginners like me!"

qa.q: How many reviews did the course have?
qa.a: Twelve thousand reviews.

qa.q: Why did Tomas feel sure enough to pay without opening the syllabus?
qa.a: Tomas took the high star count and huge number of reviews as proof the course was good, so checking seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: What did Mateo's question "Good for who?" point to, and what could Tomas do differently next time?
qa.a: It pointed to fit: a course can be great for beginners and wrong for someone with experience. Next time Tomas could read a few reviews and the syllabus before paying.

qa.q: How might the reviewer who wrote "Perfect for total beginners" see the same course?
qa.a: For that reviewer the course was exactly right, so the stars were honest; they just described a different learner from Tomas.

grounding: A young man pays for the top-rated course by star count without checking whether it suits him.

passage: The registration hall at the college was noisy, one desk per elective. The queue for Film Studies snaked past the notice board; the Urban Ecology desk had three students and a tired professor. "Film Studies," Sahil said, joining the tail. "Look at that line. Everyone knows something." Dolma stopped at the ecology desk and picked up the course outline. "Did you read what Film Studies involves?" "Watching films, obviously." "It's four written critiques and a long end-term paper. You hate writing essays." Sahil shrugged. "Then why is everyone in the queue?" Dolma looked along the line. "Because the queue was long when they got here." Sahil stayed where he was anyway, shuffling forward with the crowd, the outline still unread.

qa.q: How many students were at the Urban Ecology desk?
qa.a: Three students.

qa.q: What did Sahil believe the long queue showed?
qa.a: Sahil felt confident the queue itself was proof that the course is good, since so many people must know something.

qa.q: What could Sahil check before reaching the front of the queue?
qa.a: Sahil could read the Film Studies outline, as Dolma did, and weigh the four critiques and long paper against a dislike of writing essays.

qa.q: How does Dolma see the queue differently from Sahil?
qa.a: Dolma sees the queue as people copying whoever was ahead of them, not as information about the course, so Dolma reads the outline instead.

grounding: A student joins the longest elective queue without reading the course, treating popularity as evidence of quality.

passage:
Hey Abhinav,
Remember when I laughed at you for spending a whole Sunday visiting PGs? Well. I picked mine in ten minutes, lying on my bed in Aligarh. The listing had 4.8 stars and more than six hundred reviews. Six hundred! I didn't read a single one, didn't ask for a video call, just paid the deposit.
The room is the size of a cupboard. The "daily cleaning" is a boy with a broom on Sundays. Last night I finally scrolled the reviews: half are three words long, posted on the same two days, and my new roommate says the owner gives a free month to anyone who rates him five.
I treated the number like proof. It was just a number.
Next time I'm doing it your way, however boring it is.
Yusuf

qa.q: How many reviews did the PG listing have?
qa.a: It had more than six hundred reviews.

qa.q: What was Yusuf thinking when paying the deposit without reading a single review?
qa.a: Yusuf felt confident, even careless, assuming so many high ratings must mean a good room, so checking seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do differently when choosing the next room?
qa.a: Read a few reviews and their dates, ask for a video call or visit, and ask current tenants, the way Abhinav did.

qa.q: How might Abhinav react to this letter, given that Yusuf once laughed at the Sunday of PG visits?
qa.a: Abhinav might feel quietly proven right but also sympathetic, and might offer to help look at the next place.

grounding: A young adult picks a room by its star rating without checking and discovers popularity was not quality.

passage: So, Harish, you asked what happened to my hair. Sit down. I'm Parul, and I trust stars far too much. Before my cousin's engagement, I searched for salons near the women's hostel where I live and picked the one with 4.9 stars and two thousand ratings. Didn't read a thing. Two thousand people, I thought, how bad can it be? I walked in and said, "Just a trim and some layers." The stylist had clearly never done layers. Forty minutes later I looked like a staircase. That night I actually read the reviews. Most were for their other branch across the city, and the recent ones for this branch said "long wait" and "careless." Everyone was rating the name, not the chair I sat in. My cousin was kind about it at the engagement. The photos were not.

qa.q: How many ratings did the salon Parul picked have?
qa.a: It had two thousand ratings and 4.9 stars.

qa.q: Why did Parul feel sure the salon would be fine without reading anything?
qa.a: She thought two thousand people couldn't be wrong, so the huge number felt like proof of quality.

qa.q: What would you advise Parul before she books the next salon?
qa.a: Read the recent reviews for that exact branch, or ask a friend whose haircut she likes, instead of trusting the star count alone.

qa.q: How might Harish see the story as Parul tells it?
qa.a: Harish might find it funny but also recognise the same habit of trusting big numbers in their own choices.

grounding: A young adult chooses a salon by star count without checking and the popularity turns out to mislead.

passage:
On the highway outside the town, two dhabas faced each other. One had forty trucks parked outside and a crowd at every table. The other had three families and an empty bench.
"The crowded one, obviously," said Ritu, pulling Dilnaz by the arm. "If everyone's there, it must be good."
They waited forty minutes for a table. The dal was watery, the rotis cold. Ritu chewed slowly.
Dilnaz looked across the road. "Those truck drivers stop there because it has the biggest parking, not because of the food. The owner of the other one told Abba last year he makes everything fresh."
Ritu frowned at her plate. She had never even thought to ask why the crowd was there.

qa.q: How long did Ritu and Dilnaz wait for a table?
qa.a: They waited forty minutes for a table.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as she chewed slowly?
qa.a: Ritu felt disappointed and a bit foolish, realising the crowd hadn't meant good food.

qa.q: What could Ritu do next time she picks a place to eat?
qa.a: She could ask why a place is busy, or check with someone who knows, instead of treating the crowd as proof of quality.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the crowded dhaba?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees it as busy because of its parking, not its food, and knows the other one cooks fresh.

grounding: A young adult picks the crowded dhaba without checking, treating popularity as evidence of quality, and is disappointed.

passage:
Emeka was scrolling through online courses in his Lagos flat. He needed to learn data analysis before his internship started. One course had 4.9 stars and 80,000 reviews. He clicked "Enrol" in seconds.
"Did you read the syllabus?" asked his flatmate Sami, looking over.
"It's got 80,000 reviews. It must be good."
Two weeks later Emeka sat with his head in his hands. The course was mostly for complete beginners, and half the tools were ones his internship didn't use.
Sami showed him a smaller course with 4.4 stars and 2,000 reviews that matched the internship tools exactly. "Fewer people, but the right people."
Emeka sighed. "I just assumed that many people couldn't be wrong."

qa.q: How many reviews did the first course have?
qa.a: It had 80,000 reviews.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he sat with his head in his hands?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and let down, having trusted the huge number of stars instead of checking if the course fit his needs.

qa.q: What could Emeka have checked before enrolling?
qa.a: He could have read the syllabus and compared it with the tools his internship actually uses.

qa.q: How does Sami see the difference between the two courses?
qa.a: Sami sees that the smaller course, with fewer reviews, fits the internship better than the popular one.

grounding: A young adult enrols in the top-rated course by star count without checking, treating popularity as proof of quality.

passage:
On elective day in the college hall, the list of electives was pinned on a board. Next to each was the number of students who'd already signed up. "Digital Marketing" had 140. "Urban Ecology" had 12.
Gautam wrote his name under Digital Marketing without reading a word. "If 140 people chose it, it's the best."
Ganga, a final-year student helping at the desk, raised an eyebrow. "You said you wanted to work on city planning."
"Yeah, but look at the numbers."
"People pick it because their friends did. The professor for Urban Ecology takes students on site visits and helped three of us get internships with the city council."
Gautam looked at the two lists. He hadn't even read what either course was about.

qa.q: How many students had signed up for Urban Ecology?
qa.a: Urban Ecology had 12.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he wrote his name under Digital Marketing?
qa.a: He felt confident and certain, trusting the number of sign-ups as proof the course was best.

qa.q: What could Gautam do before finalising his elective?
qa.a: He could read both course descriptions and ask seniors like Ganga which one fits his interest in city planning.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Gautam's choice?
qa.a: Ganga seems surprised and a bit concerned, knowing Urban Ecology suits his goals better than the popular choice.

grounding: A young adult picks the most popular elective by sign-up count without reading about it, treating popularity as evidence of quality.

passage:
Lalit, let me tell you about our Manali trip dinner, since you keep asking why I'm off rajma. I'm Vandana, and on the first night we walked down the Mall Road, hungry and cold. One place had a queue out of the door, so I said, "That's the one. Look at the crowd!"
We waited fifty minutes. Fifty! Meanwhile the little dhaba next door was nearly empty; an old man was stirring a pot, and it smelled amazing. We didn't even look at its menu. When we finally sat down, the rajma was cold and too salty, and the waiter was rushed.
Walking back, I saw a family leaving the empty dhaba, all smiling. I still don't know if it was good. I just know I never checked.

qa.q: How long did they wait at the crowded restaurant?
qa.a: Fifty minutes.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel walking back past the dhaba?
qa.a: Vandana felt regretful and curious, wondering what was missed by trusting the crowd without checking.

qa.q: What could Vandana do next time in a new town?
qa.a: Look at a menu or ask a local before joining a queue, instead of treating the crowd as proof of quality.

qa.q: What might the dhaba owner think about the queue next door?
qa.a: The old man might feel frustrated or resigned, seeing people choose the crowd without trying his food.

grounding: A young adult describes picking the crowded restaurant simply because of the queue, treating popularity as proof of quality.

June: Kamal chose the GATE coaching centre with 4.8 stars and a huge banner of toppers. "Everyone's joining this one," he told Yogesh, who had suggested a smaller class run by a retired professor. "Nobody's heard of that."
August: Kamal sat in the back row of a hall with two hundred students. The teacher spoke into a mic and left right after. Doubts had to be emailed; replies took a week.
October: Yogesh showed Kamal his notebook from the small class: fourteen students, questions answered on the spot, weekly tests marked by hand. Kamal flipped through it quietly. "Four point eight stars," he muttered. "From whom, though?"

qa.q: How many students were in Yogesh's small class?

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he flipped through Yogesh's notebook?

qa.q: What could Kamal have done in June?
qa.a: Sit in on a trial class at both places and ask current students, rather than choosing by stars and banners.

qa.q: How did Yogesh experience the small class?
qa.a: Yogesh got close attention, with questions answered on the spot and weekly tests marked by hand.

passage: Swati, you're choosing your college hostel by stars on the phone? Sit, let your Tushar Mama tell you about Shimla, 1994. I was twenty, on my first trip with three friends. passage: On Saturday evening in Lajpat Nagar, the queue at the momo stall ran past the shoe shop. The stall next to it, with the same steaming baskets, had two customers. 'This one,' Pranav said, joining the long line. 'Look at the crowd. Must be the best in Delhi.' Aparna glanced at the quiet stall. The cook there was folding each momo by hand. 'Did you read anything about it?' 'Don't need to. Queue says it all.' Twenty-five minutes later they had a plate each. Pranav bit in. The filling was mostly cabbage, the chutney watery. He chewed slowly and kept smiling. 'Good, na?' Aparna noticed a college group in matching T-shirts filling half the queue, all laughing at a phone. She bought one plate from the quiet stall on the way out. It was better. She didn't say so.

qa.q: What was mostly in the filling of Pranav's momos?
qa.a: The filling was mostly cabbage.

qa.q: Why did Pranav keep smiling while chewing slowly?
qa.a: Pranav probably felt a little disappointed but didn't want to admit it, having been so sure the queue meant quality.

qa.q: What could Pranav try next time he chooses by a crowd?
qa.a: He could ask why the crowd is there, or taste a small plate from each stall, instead of taking the queue as proof.

qa.q: How does Aparna see the queue?
qa.a: Aparna sees that the crowd was partly one college group, not a sign of quality, and quietly finds the other stall better.

grounding: A young adult picks the crowded food stall without checking, treating popularity as evidence that it is the best.
